source.title: The Surprising Harmfulness of Benign Overfitting for Adversarial Robustness

record.file_problem: Full text is present; no apparent cutoff or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: Uses benign overfitting as the setting for analyzing adversarial risk, but does not test the claim versions about random-label fitting, training time, unstructured inputs, label-noise sweeps, regularization effects on random-label fitting, or learning order.
record.gate_note: The paper analyzes noisy-data regression and its adversarial risk. It does not measure the claim’s random-label image-classification behavior. Its results on standard and adversarial risk are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper analyzes standard and adversarial excess risk in noisy linear regression and a linearized two-layer NTK model. It does not test any specified random-label claim. Noisy-target interpolation provides the setting, but is not a test of completely random labeling, optimization time, input randomization, corruption sweeps, explicit regularization as specified, or learning order.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: under specified conditions, benignly overfitted linear and two-layer NTK estimators achieve vanishing standard excess risk but diverging adversarial risk despite robust ground truth. More precisely, the ridge theorem concerns a trade-off between the standard-risk convergence rate relative to ridgeless regression and bounded adversarial risk.
record.recipe_differences: Theoretical analysis of linear regression and two-layer NTK models with noisy regression targets; it does not reproduce random-label image-classification experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The conclusions are stated under specified benign-overfitting, noise, and high-dimension conditions; the ridge trade-off additionally requires Condition 2.

fits_no_version.finding: Under Condition 1 and the specified noise lower bound, ridgeless linear regression has vanishing standard excess risk and diverging adversarial risk divided by α².
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign interpolation of noisy regression targets can cause unbounded adversarial vulnerability despite consistent standard prediction.

fits_no_version.finding: Under Conditions 1 and 2 and the specified noise lower bound, the sum of normalized standard risk and normalized adversarial risk diverges for every ridge parameter.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ridge regression cannot retain the specified ridgeless standard-risk convergence rate while keeping adversarial risk bounded under the theorem's conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Under Conditions 3 and 4, the linearized two-layer NTK gradient-descent solution has vanishing standard excess risk and diverging adversarial risk divided by α².
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign overfitting in the specified NTK regime can coexist with unbounded adversarial vulnerability.

record.problems: The results are theoretical and conditional on stated assumptions; the authors identify relaxing the NTK high-dimension condition and studying more complex models such as Transformers as open questions.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling fitted by standard deep networks using stochastic gradient methods, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true and random labels, and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Zero training error on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across a clean-to-fully-random label corruption sweep.
Weight decay, dropout, and augmentation effects on random-label fitting, and true-label generalization after removing these regularizers.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy labels, and differences in learning trajectories.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T4 classification overstates its connection to the specified claims: the paper studies a related regression phenomenon rather than using a random-label claim as a tool. Row states here describe whether their measures establish a claim-version effect; they do not dispute the reported theoretical risk results.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random image labels, test error at chance, standard deep networks, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for random versus true labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
A sweep from clean to fully corrupted labels, perfect training fit across the sweep, and the test-error trend.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
Whether real patterns are learned before noisy or random labels, and whether they are learned differently over time.
